conclusion: Similar test statistics at linked SNPs make it difficult to distinguish the causal variant from its proxies.
scope: Motivates study design for causal-variant localization rather than discovery of an associated locus.
span: Test statistics calculated in a follow-up study over tightly linked SNPs will behave similarly, and thus it is difficult to distinguish between the causal variant and its proxies.

objects: Z vector; noncentrality lambda_c sqrt(N); SNP correlation matrix Sigma
assumptions: specified causal SNP c; known regional allele frequencies and SNP correlations; additive case-control model
conclusion: Regional association Z scores are modeled by an MVN with LD covariance and a mean propagated from the causal SNP through its SNP correlations, enabling direct Monte Carlo draws.
scope: Single-population association-score distribution used to replace explicit case-control panel simulation.
span: We therefore add upon the observation made by Han et al.【24†^{5}】 and Conneely et al.,【25†^{6}】 who noticed that the distribution of Z = Z_{1}, Z_{2}, …, Z_{k} follows an MVN distribution $Z\sim \mathcal{N}\left(\Lambda \sqrt{N},\Sigma \right)$, in which $\lambda \sqrt{N}=\left({r}_{1c}{\lambda }_{c}\sqrt{N},{r}_{2c}{\lambda }_{c}\sqrt{N},\dots ,{r}_{kc}{\lambda }_{c}\sqrt{N}\right)$ and Σ is the k × k variance-covariance matrix of the SNPs in which the i^{th}, j^{th} entry of Σ is the correlation coefficient of SNPs s_{i}, s_{j}. Given a region of the genome where the MAFs and correlations of the SNPs are known, we can replace the simulation approach by a simple Monte Carlo sampling from the corresponding MVN distribution.

objects: weighted Z-score vector T; N_j; population means Lambda_j sqrt(N_j); LD covariance Sigma_j
assumptions: independent studies; per-study MVN model; balanced case-control presentation; weights proportional to sqrt(N_j)
conclusion: The weighted-Z meta-analysis vector is MVN with the weighted noncentrality mean and sample-size-weighted average of the population LD covariance matrices.
scope: Distributional consequence of the stated model; no finite-sample error bound for the MVN approximation is given.
span: Because each Z_{i}, _{j} is normally distributed with a mean of λ_{i}, _{j} and a variance of 1, T_{i} is also normally distributed, with a mean of ${\sum }_{j}\sqrt{{N}_{j}}{\lambda }_{i,j}\sqrt{{N}_{j}}/\sqrt{{\sum }_{j}{N}_{j}}$ and a variance of 1. Therefore, the distribution of T = (T_{1}, T_{2}, …, T_{k}) will also be MVN: $$T\sim \mathcal{N}\left(\frac{{\sum }_{j}\sqrt{{N}_{j}}{\Lambda }_{j}\sqrt{{N}_{j}}}{\sqrt{{\sum }_{j}{N}_{j}}},\frac{{\sum }_{j}{N}_{j}{\Sigma }_{j}}{{\sum }_{j}{N}_{j}}\right)\text{.}$$  | (Equation 1)

objects: q_i; observed original-study Z scores; empirical relative risks; SNP correlation matrix
assumptions: one candidate SNP is causal at a time; relative risks estimated from the original study; fixed-effects assumption
conclusion: Causal-SNP design prior weights are formed by normalizing the MVN densities of the original Z scores under each candidate-causal hypothesis.
scope: Empirical design prior over causal identities; not a shrinkage prior on multiple regression effects.
span: Now, under the assumption that s_{i} is causal, Z^{∗} is drawn from the MVN distribution $Z\sim \mathcal{N}\left(\Lambda \sqrt{{N}^{\prime }},\Sigma \right)$, in which $\lambda \sqrt{N}=\left({r}_{1i}{\lambda }_{i}\sqrt{{N}^{\prime }},\dots ,{r}_{ki}{\lambda }_{i}\sqrt{{N}^{\prime }}\right)$. For each SNP s_{i}, we compute q_{i}, the MVN probability density function of the observed Z scores Z^{∗} under Z given that s_{i} is causal, and normalize these so that they sum to 1. These q_{1}, q_{2}, …, q_{k} serve as the prior probabilities that each SNP is causal.

objects: design D; population sample allocations; expected LSR
assumptions: fixed total sample budget; specified candidate populations; expected LSR evaluated for each grid design
conclusion: Grid search chooses the population allocation with maximum estimated expected LSR among designs on the grid.
scope: Gridwise optimum only; enumeration is feasible when the number of populations is not too large.
span: Our method identifies the best fine-mapping study design by using a grid-search algorithm over all possible designs D; this grid search is feasible when the number of populations involved is not too large. The final design chosen is the D with the maximum expected LSR out of all designs on the grid.

objects: target regions; prior-study regional test statistics; population reference data
assumptions: follow-up study designed from previous association evidence
conclusion: The framework uses target regions, earlier SNP association statistics and population reference data to select follow-up sample allocations under a budget.
scope: Inputs to the statistical design framework; includes prior-study information and reference LD rather than newly observed follow-up outcomes.
span: We incorporated our analytical framework into a software package called MULTIPOP, which takes as an input a set of regions, test statistics obtained for the SNPs in these regions in previous studies of the phenotype (used as priors), and a set of reference data sets from the available populations. MULTIPOP uses this information to decide how many samples of each population should be further studied so that the LSR of detection of a causal SNP will be maximized under budget constraints.

objects: localization success rate; causal-SNP rank; regional p-value ordering
assumptions: specified causal variant; repeated study draws; random tie breaking for rank
conclusion: Localization is evaluated by the frequency that the causal SNP has the lowest regional p value or by its average rank with random tie breaking.
scope: The second metric is a rank expectation rather than an event probability.
span: The first measure of LSR computes the fraction of study samples in which the causal variant has the lowest p value among all SNPs in the region. This corresponds to the scenario in which exactly one SNP from each region is undergoing functional analysis; we therefore measure the fraction of regions in which the actual causal variant will be chosen for the functional analysis. The second measure that we use is the average rank of the causal variant when the SNPs are ordered from lowest to highest p value with ties broken randomly.

objects: additive disease model; one causal SNP; weighted-Z meta-analysis statistic
conclusion: The demonstrated analysis covers an additive disease model with one causal SNP and one particular meta-analysis statistic, and deviations require another analysis.
scope: No general guarantee for multiple causal variants, alternative genetic models or different meta-analysis statistics.
span: It is important to realize that the results demonstrated here by no means cover all possible scenarios of follow-up studies. Particularly, our analysis corresponds to an additive disease model with one causal SNP, and we treat one specific meta-analysis statistic. Any deviation from this scenario requires another similar analysis.

span: Although the majority of causal variants have a fixed effect size across all populations,【22†^{3}】 a significant percentage will show a heterogeneous effect across different populations.
